newsitem.title: USA: New home sales plunge confirms slow growth.
newsitem.headline: New home sales plunge confirms slow growth.

text.p: New home sales tumbled in October and a key economic forecasting gauge barely crept higher, reports showed Tuesday, as evidence mounted that slow growth will extend into next year.

Sales of new homes fell 8.7 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 714,000 in October after falling 4.5 percent in September, the Commerce Department said. It was the steepest drop in seven months.
The department said the back-to-back declines also brought sales to the lowest annual rate in seven months, since new homes changed hands at a rate of 713,000 in March.
The Conference Board said in a separate report that its Index of Leading Indicators edged up 0.1 percent in October -- the ninth straight rise after a revised 0.2 percent September increase.

The index, compiled by the New York-based business research group from 11 separate measures of economic activity, is supposed to foreshadow trends six to nine months ahead, though many analysts wonder about its forecasting value.
"It does suggest that economic activity has slowed markedly and the fourth quarter growth rate will not be robust," said economist Joel Naroff of First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C.
The government previously reported that the economy grew at a 2 percent annual rate in the third quarter, much slower than the second quarter's brisk 4.7 percent pace of growth.

Signs of more modest growth boost the chances that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates steady, analysts said, a prospect welcomed by investors after reports on Monday showed surprising strength in manufacturing and construction.

Investors have bid stock prices to record highs on signs of modest but steady economic growth, which is expected to fuel corporate profits, and any indication of a surge in growth that could fuel inflation could lead to a big sell-off.
Federal Reserve Gov. Edward Kelley, speaking to reporters after addressing a conference on banking issues, said he expected moderate growth.

"As far as I can see, we seem to be moving along without undue identifiable surges or air pockets, which would indicate to me that the most likely thing would be for another quarter of about trend growth," Kelley said.
The Fed, the nation's central bank, defines trend growth as an annual rate between 2 percent and 2.25 percent, enough to create jobs but not fire up wage and price pressures.

The drop in October new home sales was the biggest since a 9.1 percent plunge in March. Previously the department had said September sales fell 0.5 percent but revised that to show a much steeper drop.

The report confirmed that the glow was gone from the housing market, as indicated a week ago when the National Association of Realtors said sales of existing homes also fell in October, the fifth straight decline.
"It's clear that housing markets have topped out, probably in August," said economist David Lereah of the Mortgage Bankers Association. "We're contracting a bit now."
Every region of the country posted lower sales of new homes in October.
The sharpest drop came in the Northeast, where sales tumbled 32.3 percent, the biggest drop since a 33.6 percent plunge in May 1993.
Sales in the Midwest fell 11.3 percent and 8.9 percent in the West. Sales in the South, the nation's largest regional market, eased 0.6 percent.
While sales have fallen, there is little chance the bottom will fall out of the housing market, since job growth remains steady and mortgage rates are falling.
Last week the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said fixed-rate home mortgage rates fell for the sixth week in a row to a nine-month low.

Thirty-year fixed-rate mortgages averaged 7.52 percent in the week ending Nov. 29, down from 7.53 percent the previous week. The rate has not been lower since the week ended March 8, when the average was 7.38 percent.
The average sales price for a new home fell to $165,300 in October from $168,400 in September.
